title: Amazon ECS Gateway Arrives with Generated Hostnames and No Custom Domain Support
gist: AWS released Amazon ECS Gateway, an account-level ingress resource that splits networking ownership between platform and application teams, but each service gets only a generated hostname with no documented custom-domain support. Community reaction was skeptical about usefulness, and documentation reveals cost and operational limits such as unconsolidated load balancers.

insights.claim: Amazon ECS Gateway is an account-level ingress resource where platform teams define networking once and application teams attach services through a gateway connector, available in all commercial regions where ECS runs at no charge beyond the resources it provisions.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS is productizing the platform-team/app-team split for container ingress.

insights.claim: Platform teams configure the gateway's IAM role, subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listeners and optional WAF web ACLs; for each service ECS then provisions an ACM certificate, hostname, listener rule, target group and a security group accepting traffic only from the load balancer.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The value proposition is organizational: central governance of ingress with self-service for app teams.
insights.locator: The split it introduces is organizational

themes.theme: Generated hostnames and missing custom domains

insights.claim: Neither the announcement nor the documentation describes how to put a custom domain in front of a gateway service; each service gets a generated hostname of the form https://<unique-id>.ecs.<region>.on.aws.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The missing custom-domain path limits use for production customer-facing traffic.
insights.quote: each service "gets a generated hostname in the form https://<unique-id>.ecs.<region>.on.aws,"

insights.claim: A CNAME would not solve the problem because the gateway creates host-based rules in the load balancer, so requests arriving under another hostname would not be routed.
insights.speaker: zurnout (Reddit commenter)
insights.so_what: Host-based routing is a structural constraint, not a missing DNS step, per a community commenter.
insights.quote: It creates host-based rules in the load balancer, so it wouldn’t know where to route if you used a CNAME.

insights.claim: Commenters see the feature as usable mainly for ephemeral or preview environments where the app is not hostname aware, not for existing production setups.
insights.speaker: ResponsibleWaltz1479 (Reddit commenter)
insights.so_what: Near-term fit is dev/preview workloads, not core production ingress.

themes.theme: Value debate: wrapper or real simplification

insights.claim: Critics call the service just an ALB and DNS wrapper that could be a CDK construct, while another commenter warns higher-level L3 constructs often become a mistake because they must expose every L2 knob and are painful to eject from.
insights.speaker: bioJesusMain (Reddit commenter)
insights.so_what: Highlights the perennial risk of opinionated abstractions on AWS primitives.
insights.quote: It’s just ALB and DNS with a wrapper

insights.claim: Supporters say letting a cloud team define networking once while application teams deploy against it is a solid improvement, with the test being whether it removes complexity without taking away too much control.
insights.speaker: Aggressive-Height167 (Reddit commenter)
insights.so_what: Adoption will hinge on control trade-offs rather than the capability itself.
insights.quote: seems like a pretty solid improvement

insights.claim: The thread's most upvoted comment dismissed the launch as a promotion project, and several commenters asked why AWS Elastic Beanstalk, which added Cluster Mode last month, did not already cover the ground.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Suggests overlapping AWS container-ingress products and customer confusion on positioning.

insights.claim: A gateway adds load balancers as existing ones fill and removes them only when empty, but does not consolidate load balancers or move services between them, so several partly filled (and billed) load balancers can remain after services leave.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: ALB count and cost scale with service count without bin-packing, a hidden cost omitted from the announcement.

insights.claim: Twenty-five services share one load balancer, with a default maxAlbCount of 10 and a documented ceiling of 200 per gateway; if the maximum is reached with no capacity, deployment fails.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Hard scale limits (about 250 services by default) constrain larger estates.
insights.quote: if maxAlbCount is reached and no ALB has available capacity, the deployment fails.

insights.claim: ECS does not repair changes made outside it, so modifying or deleting a managed resource can stop traffic and cause later deployments, gateway updates and cleanup to fail.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Operational fragility toward out-of-band changes raises governance requirements.
insights.quote: does not repair changes made outside it

insights.claim: Listeners serve HTTPS on port 443 only, services must use awsvpc networking in the same VPC and account, and Express Mode services are excluded.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Narrow compatibility reduces the addressable base of existing ECS workloads.
